findings.title: Denial entries prevent the intended database refresh after permissions change
findings.body: A cached denial is returned before checking the permission cache or re-querying the database, and nothing in this change invalidates `permDenialCache` when a resource or permission is created. Consequently, if a check for a known dashboard/folder UID is denied before its permission is written, all subsequent checks for that same UID remain denied for `shortCacheTTL` (30 seconds), even though the database now grants access. This bypasses the newly added stale-cache fallback and can still prevent creators from accessing newly created resources. Denial entries need invalidation on permission/resource changes or must not be used when freshness is required.

findings.title: Denial cache conflates anonymous and renderer identities
findings.body: The denial key includes only `UserUID`, not `IdentityType` or the full subject. Anonymous and renderer subjects both commonly use ID `0` (as represented by `anonymous:0` and `render:0`), so an anonymous denial for a dashboard read stores the same key later used by the renderer. The renderer request will then return the cached denial instead of its built-in read-all permission for up to 30 seconds. Include the identity type/full subject in the key.

findings.title: Delimited denial-cache key is ambiguous for resource and folder UIDs
findings.body: `name` and `parent` are concatenated with `_` without escaping or length-prefixing. Since dashboard and folder UIDs can contain underscores, distinct pairs such as name `dash_a` with parent `folder` and name `dash` with parent `a_folder` generate the same cache key. A denial for one resource context can therefore incorrectly deny access to the other until expiry. Use an unambiguous encoding (for example JSON, escaped components, or length-prefixed fields).
